Working together as an <color=#3366CC>interdisciplinary team</color>, many <color=#3366CC>health professionals</color> besides medical practitioners are involved in
the delivery of modern health care. Examples include: <color=#3366CC>nurses</color>, <color=#3366CC>emergency medical technicians</color> and <color=#3366CC>paramedics</color>,
laboratory scientists, <color=#3366CC>pharmacists</color>, podiatrists, <color=#3366CC>physiotherapists</color>, respiratory therapists, <color=#3366CC>speech therapists</color>, occupational
therapists, radiographers, dietitians, and <color=#3366CC>bioengineers</color>, medical physicists, <color=#3366CC>surgeons</color>, surgeon's assistant, surgical
technologist.
The scope and sciences underpinning human medicine overlap many other fields. A patient admitted to the hospital is
usually under the care of a specific team based on their main presenting problem, e.g., the <color=#3366CC>cardiology</color> team, who then
may interact with other specialties, e.g., <color=#3366CC>surgical</color>, <color=#3366CC>radiology</color>, to help diagnose or treat the main problem or any
subsequent complications/developments.
Physicians have many specializations and sub specializations into certain branches of medicine, which are listed
below. There are variations from country to country regarding which specialties certain subspecialties are in.
The main branches of medicine are:
• Basic sciences of medicine; this is what every physician is educated in, and some return to in biomedical research.
• <color=#3366CC>Interdisciplinary fields</color>, where different medical specialties are mixed to function in certain occasions.
• <color=#3366CC>Medical specialties</color>
Basic sciences
• <color=#3366CC>Anatomy</color> is the study of the physical structure of <color=#3366CC>organisms</color>. In contrast to macroscopic or gross anatomy, <color=#3366CC>cytology</color>
and <color=#3366CC>histology</color> are concerned with microscopic structures.
• <color=#3366CC>Biochemistry</color> is the study of the chemistry taking place in living organisms, especially the structure and function of
their chemical components.
• <color=#3366CC>Biomechanics</color> is the study of the structure and function of biological systems by means of the methods of
<color=#3366CC>Mechanics</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Biophysics</color> is an interdisciplinary science that uses the methods of <color=#3366CC>physics</color> and <color=#3366CC>physical chemistry</color> to study
biological systems.
• Biostatistics is the application of <color=#3366CC>statistics</color> to biological fields in the broadest sense. A knowledge of biostatistics is
essential in the planning, evaluation, and interpretation of medical research. It is also fundamental to <color=#3366CC>epidemiology</color>
and evidence-based medicine.
• <color=#3366CC>Cytology</color> is the microscopic study of individual <color=#3366CC>cells</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Embryology</color> is the study of the early development of organisms.
• <color=#3366CC>Endocrinology</color> is the study of <color=#3366CC>hormones</color> and their effect throughout the body of animals.
• <color=#3366CC>Epidemiology</color> is the study of the demographics of disease processes, and includes, but is not limited to, the study
of <color=#3366CC>epidemics</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Genetics</color> is the study of genes, and their role in <color=#3366CC>biological inheritance</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Gynecology</color> is the study of female reproductive system.

• <color=#3366CC>Histology</color> is the study of the structures of <color=#3366CC>biological tissues</color> by light <color=#3366CC>microscopy</color>, <color=#3366CC>electron microscopy</color> and
immunohistochemistry.
• <color=#3366CC>Immunology</color> is the study of the <color=#3366CC>immune system</color>, which includes the innate and adaptive immune system in
humans, for example.
• Lifestyle medicine is the study of the <color=#3366CC>chronic conditions</color>, and how to prevent, treat and reverse them.
• Medical physics is the study of the applications of physics principles in medicine.

• <color=#3366CC>Microbiology</color> is the study of cellular, multicellular, and acellular <color=#3366CC>microorganisms</color> such as <color=#3366CC>protozoa</color>, <color=#3366CC>bacteria</color>, <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>,
<color=#3366CC>viruses</color>, <color=#3366CC>prions</color>, and viroids.

• <color=#3366CC>Molecular biology</color> is the study of molecular underpinnings of the process of <color=#3366CC>replication</color>, <color=#3366CC>transcription</color> and <color=#3366CC>translation</color>
of the genetic material.
• <color=#3366CC>Neuroscience</color> includes those disciplines of science that are related to the study of the <color=#3366CC>nervous system</color>. A main
focus of neuroscience is the <color=#3366CC>biology</color> and <color=#3366CC>physiology</color> of the human brain and <color=#3366CC>spinal cord</color>. Some related clinical
specialties include <color=#3366CC>neurology</color>, <color=#3366CC>neurosurgery</color> and <color=#3366CC>psychiatry</color>.
• Nutrition science (theoretical focus) and dietetics (practical focus) is the study of the relationship of food and drink
to health and disease, especially in determining an optimal diet. Medical nutrition therapy is done by dietitians and

is prescribed for <color=#3366CC>diabetes</color>, <color=#3366CC>cardiovascular diseases</color>, weight and eating <color=#3366CC>disorders</color>, <color=#3366CC>allergies</color>, <color=#3366CC>malnutrition</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>neoplastic</color> diseases.
• <color=#3366CC>Pathology as a science</color> is the study of <color=#3366CC>disease</color> – the causes, course, progression and resolution thereof.
• <color=#3366CC>Pharmacology</color> is the study of <color=#3366CC>drugs</color> and their actions.
• Photobiology is the study of the interactions between non-ionizing radiation and living organisms.
• <color=#3366CC>Physiology</color> is the study of the normal functioning of the body and the underlying regulatory mechanisms.
• Radiobiology is the study of the interactions between <color=#3366CC>ionizing radiation</color> and living organisms.
• <color=#3366CC>Toxicology</color> is the study of hazardous effects of drugs and <color=#3366CC>poisons</color>.
Specialties
In the broadest meaning of "medicine", there are many different specialties. In the UK, most specialities have their own
body or college, which has its own entrance examination. These are collectively known as the Royal Colleges, although
not all currently use the term "Royal". The development of a speciality is often driven by new technology (such as the
development of effective anaesthetics) or ways of working (such as emergency departments); the new specialty leads
to the formation of a unifying body of doctors and the prestige of administering their own examination.
Within medical circles, specialities usually fit into one of two broad categories: "Medicine" and "Surgery". "Medicine"
refers to the practice of non-operative medicine, and most of its subspecialties require preliminary training in Internal
Medicine. In the UK, this was traditionally evidenced by passing the examination for the Membership of the Royal
College of Physicians (MRCP) or the equivalent college in Scotland or Ireland. "Surgery" refers to the practice of
operative medicine, and most subspecialties in this area require preliminary training in General Surgery, which in the
UK leads to membership of the Royal College of Surgeons of England (MRCS). At present, some specialties of
medicine do not fit easily into either of these categories, such as radiology, pathology, or anesthesia. Most of these
have branched from one or other of the two camps above; for example anaesthesia developed first as a faculty of the
Royal College of Surgeons (for which MRCS/FRCS would have been required) before becoming the Royal College of
Anaesthetists and membership of the college is attained by sitting for the examination of the Fellowship of the Royal
College of Anesthetists (FRCA).
Surgical specialty
Surgery is an ancient medical specialty that uses operative manual and instrumental techniques on a patient to
investigate or treat a <color=#3366CC>pathological</color> condition such as disease or <color=#3366CC>injury</color>, to help improve bodily function or appearance or
to repair unwanted ruptured areas (for example, a perforated ear drum). Surgeons must also manage pre-operative,
post-operative, and potential surgical candidates on the hospital wards. In some centers, <color=#3366CC>anesthesiology</color> is part of the
division of surgery (for historical and logistical reasons), although it is not a surgical discipline. Other medical specialties
may employ surgical procedures, such as <color=#3366CC>ophthalmology</color> and <color=#3366CC>dermatology</color>, but are not considered surgical
sub-specialties per se.
Surgical training in the U.S. requires a minimum of five years of residency after medical school. Sub-specialties of
surgery often require seven or more years. In addition, fellowships can last an additional one to three years. Because
post-residency fellowships can be competitive, many trainees devote two additional years to research. Thus in some
cases surgical training will not finish until more than a decade after medical school. Furthermore, surgical training can
be very difficult and time-consuming.
Surgical subspecialties include those a physician may specialize in after undergoing general surgery residency training
as well as several surgical fields with separate residency training. Surgical subspecialties that one may pursue
following general surgery residency training:
• <color=#3366CC>Bariatric surgery</color>
• Cardiovascular surgery – may also be pursued through a separate cardiovascular surgery residency track
• Colorectal surgery
• Endocrine surgery
• General surgery
• Hand surgery
• Hepato-pancreato-biliary surgery
• Minimally invasive surgery
• Pediatric surgery
• <color=#3366CC>Plastic surgery</color> – may also be pursued through a separate plastic surgery residency track
• Surgical critical care
• Surgical oncology
• <color=#3366CC>Transplant surgery</color>
• Trauma surgery
• Vascular surgery – may also be pursued through a separate vascular surgery residency track
Other surgical specialties within medicine with their own individual residency training:
• <color=#3366CC>Dermatology</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Neurosurgery</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Ophthalmology</color>
• Oral and maxillofacial surgery
• <color=#3366CC>Orthopedic surgery</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Otorhinolaryngology</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Podiatric surgery</color> – do not undergo medical school training, but rather separate training in podiatry school
• <color=#3366CC>Urology</color>
Internal medicine specialty
Internal medicine is the <color=#3366CC>medical specialty</color> dealing with the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of adult diseases.
According to some sources, an emphasis on internal structures is implied. In North America, specialists in internal
medicine are commonly called "internists". Elsewhere, especially in <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth</color> nations, such specialists are often
called <color=#3366CC>physicians</color>. These terms, internist or physician (in the narrow sense, common outside North America), generally
exclude practitioners of gynecology and obstetrics, pathology, psychiatry, and especially surgery and its
subspecialities.
Because their patients are often seriously ill or require complex investigations, internists do much of their work in
hospitals. Formerly, many internists were not subspecialized; such general physicians would see any complex
nonsurgical problem; this style of practice has become much less common. In modern urban practice, most internists
are subspecialists: that is, they generally limit their medical practice to problems of one organ system or to one
particular area of medical knowledge. For example, <color=#3366CC>gastroenterologists</color> and <color=#3366CC>nephrologists</color> specialize respectively in
diseases of the gut and the kidneys.
In the Commonwealth of Nations and some other countries, specialist <color=#3366CC>pediatricians</color> and <color=#3366CC>geriatricians</color> are also described
as specialist physicians (or internists) who have subspecialized by age of patient rather than by organ system.
Elsewhere, especially in North America, general pediatrics is often a form of primary care.
There are many subspecialities (or subdisciplines) of <color=#3366CC>internal medicine</color>:

*<color=#3366CC>Angiology</color>/Vascular Medicine *Bariatrics *<color=#3366CC>Cardiology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Critical care medicine</color> *<color=#3366CC>Endocrinology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Gastroenterology</color>

*<color=#3366CC>Geriatrics</color> *<color=#3366CC>Hematology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Hepatology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Infectious disease</color> *<color=#3366CC>Nephrology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Neurology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Oncology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Pediatrics</color>
*<color=#3366CC>Pulmonology</color>/Pneumology/Respirology/chest medicine *<color=#3366CC>Rheumatology</color> *<color=#3366CC>Sports Medicine</color>
Training in internal medicine (as opposed to surgical training), varies considerably across the world: see the articles on
<color=#3366CC>medical education</color> for more details. In North America, it requires at least three years of residency training after medical
school, which can then be followed by a one- to three-year fellowship in the subspecialties listed above. In general,
resident work hours in medicine are less than those in surgery, averaging about 60 hours per week in the US. This
difference does not apply in the UK where all doctors are now required by law to work less than 48 hours per week on
average.
Diagnostic specialties
• <color=#3366CC>Clinical laboratory</color> sciences are the clinical diagnostic services that apply laboratory techniques to diagnosis and
management of patients. In the United States, these services are supervised by a pathologist. The personnel that
work in these <color=#3366CC>medical laboratory</color> departments are technically trained staff who do not hold medical degrees, but
who usually hold an undergraduate medical technology degree, who actually perform the <color=#3366CC>tests</color>, assays, and
procedures needed for providing the specific services. Subspecialties include transfusion medicine, cellular
pathology, clinical chemistry, <color=#3366CC>hematology</color>, <color=#3366CC>clinical microbiology</color>, and <color=#3366CC>clinical immunology</color>.
• Clinical neurophysiology is concerned with testing the physiology or function of the central and peripheral aspects
of the nervous system. These kinds of tests can be divided into recordings of: (1) spontaneous or continuously
running electrical activity, or (2) stimulus evoked responses. Subspecialties include <color=#3366CC>electroencephalography</color>,
electromyography, evoked potential, nerve conduction study, and polysomnography. Sometimes these tests are
performed by techs without a medical degree, but the interpretation of these tests is done by a medical
professional.
• Diagnostic <color=#3366CC>radiology</color> is concerned with imaging of the body, e.g. by <color=#3366CC>x-rays</color>, x-ray <color=#3366CC>computed tomography</color>,
<color=#3366CC>ultrasonography</color>, and <color=#3366CC>nuclear magnetic resonance</color> tomography. Interventional radiologists can access areas in the
body under imaging for an intervention or diagnostic sampling.
• <color=#3366CC>Nuclear medicine</color> is concerned with studying human organ systems by administering radiolabelled substances
(radiopharmaceuticals) to the body, which can then be imaged outside the body by a gamma camera or a PET
scanner. Each radiopharmaceutical consists of two parts: a tracer that is specific for the function under study (e.g.,
neurotransmitter pathway, metabolic pathway, blood flow, or other), and a radionuclide (usually either a
gamma-emitter or a positron emitter). There is a degree of overlap between nuclear medicine and radiology, as
evidenced by the emergence of combined devices such as the PET/CT scanner.
• <color=#3366CC>Pathology as a medical specialty</color> is the branch of medicine that deals with the study of diseases and the
morphologic, physiologic changes produced by them. As a diagnostic specialty, pathology can be considered the
basis of modern scientific medical knowledge and plays a large role in evidence-based medicine. Many modern
molecular tests such as flow cytometry, <color=#3366CC>polymerase chain reaction</color> (PCR), immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics,
gene rearrangements studies, and fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) fall within the territory of pathology.
Other major specialties
The following are some major medical specialties that do not directly fit into any of the above-mentioned groups:
• <color=#3366CC>Anesthesiology</color> (also known as anaesthetics): concerned with the perioperative management of the surgical
patient. The anesthesiologist's role during surgery is to prevent derangement in the vital organs' (i.e. brain, heart,
kidneys) functions and postoperative pain. Outside of the operating room, the anesthesiology physician also serves
the same function in the labor and delivery ward, and some are specialized in critical medicine.
• <color=#3366CC>Emergency medicine</color> is concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of acute or life-threatening conditions,
including <color=#3366CC>trauma</color>, surgical, medical, pediatric, and psychiatric emergencies.
• <color=#3366CC>Family medicine</color>, <color=#3366CC>family practice</color>, general practice or primary care is, in many countries, the first port-of-call for
patients with non-emergency medical problems. Family physicians often provide services across a broad range of
settings including office based practices, emergency department coverage, inpatient care, and nursing home care.
• <color=#3366CC>Medical genetics</color> is concerned with the diagnosis and management of hereditary disorders.
• <color=#3366CC>Neurology</color> is concerned with diseases of the nervous system. In the UK, neurology is a subspecialty of general
medicine.
• <color=#3366CC>Obstetrics</color> and <color=#3366CC>gynecology</color> (often abbreviated as <color=#3366CC>OB/GYN</color> (American English) or Obs & Gynae (British English))
are concerned respectively with childbirth and the female reproductive and associated organs. <color=#3366CC>Reproductive</color>
<color=#3366CC>medicine</color> and fertility medicine are generally practiced by gynecological specialists.
• <color=#3366CC>Pediatrics</color> (AE) or paediatrics (BE) is devoted to the care of infants, children, and adolescents. Like internal
medicine, there are many pediatric subspecialties for specific age ranges, organ systems, disease classes, and
sites of care delivery.
• Pharmaceutical medicine is the medical scientific discipline concerned with the discovery, development, evaluation,
registration, monitoring and medical aspects of marketing of medicines for the benefit of patients and public health.
• Physical medicine and rehabilitation (or physiatry) is concerned with functional improvement after injury, illness, or
<color=#3366CC>congenital disorders</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Podiatric medicine</color> is the study of, diagnosis, and medical and surgical treatment of disorders of the foot, ankle,
lower limb, hip and lower back.
• <color=#3366CC>Preventive medicine</color> is the branch of medicine concerned with preventing disease.
• Community health or <color=#3366CC>public health</color> is an aspect of health services concerned with threats to the overall health of a
community based on population health analysis.
• <color=#3366CC>Psychiatry</color> is the branch of medicine concerned with the bio-psycho-social study of the etiology, diagnosis,

treatment and prevention of <color=#3366CC>cognitive</color>, <color=#3366CC>perceptual</color>, <color=#3366CC>emotional</color> and <color=#3366CC>behavioral</color> disorders. Related fields include
<color=#3366CC>psychotherapy</color> and <color=#3366CC>clinical psychology</color>.
Interdisciplinary fields
Some interdisciplinary sub-specialties of medicine include:
• Addiction medicine deals with the treatment of addiction.
• Aerospace medicine deals with medical problems related to flying and space travel.
• <color=#3366CC>Biomedical Engineering</color> is a field dealing with the application of <color=#3366CC>engineering</color> principles to medical practice.
• Clinical pharmacology is concerned with how systems of <color=#3366CC>therapeutics</color> interact with patients.
• Conservation medicine studies the relationship between human and non-human animal health, and environmental
conditions. Also known as ecological medicine, environmental medicine, or medical geology.
• Disaster medicine deals with medical aspects of emergency preparedness, disaster mitigation and management.
• Diving medicine (or hyperbaric medicine) is the prevention and treatment of diving-related problems.
• Evolutionary medicine is a perspective on medicine derived through applying <color=#3366CC>evolutionary</color> theory.
• Forensic medicine deals with medical questions in <color=#3366CC>legal</color> context, such as determination of the time and cause of
death, type of weapon used to inflict trauma, reconstruction of the facial features using remains of deceased (skull)
thus aiding identification.
• Gender-based medicine studies the biological and physiological differences between the human sexes and how
that affects differences in disease.
• Health informatics is a relatively recent field that deal with the application of computers and <color=#3366CC>information technology</color>
to medicine.
• Hospice and Palliative Medicine is a relatively modern branch of clinical medicine that deals with pain and symptom
relief and emotional support in patients with terminal illnesses including cancer and <color=#3366CC>heart failure</color>.
• Hospital medicine is the general medical care of hospitalized patients. Physicians whose primary professional
focus is hospital medicine are called hospitalists in the United States and <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>. The term Most Responsible
Physician (MRP) or attending physician is also used interchangeably to describe this role.
• Laser medicine involves the use of lasers in the diagnostics or treatment of various conditions.
• Many other health science fields, e.g. dietetics
• <color=#3366CC>Medical ethics</color> deals with <color=#3366CC>ethical</color> and moral principles that apply values and judgments to the practice of medicine.

• <color=#3366CC>Medical humanities</color> includes the <color=#3366CC>humanities</color> (<color=#3366CC>literature</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>ethics</color>, history and religion), <color=#3366CC>social science</color>

(<color=#3366CC>anthropology</color>, <color=#3366CC>cultural studies</color>, <color=#3366CC>psychology</color>, <color=#3366CC>sociology</color>), and the arts (<color=#3366CC>literature</color>, theater, film, and <color=#3366CC>visual arts</color>) and
their application to <color=#3366CC>medical education</color> and practice.
• Nosokinetics is the science/subject of measuring and modelling the process of care in health and social care
systems.
• Nosology is the classification of diseases for various purposes.
• <color=#3366CC>Occupational medicine</color> is the provision of health advice to organizations and individuals to ensure that the highest
standards of health and safety at work can be achieved and maintained.
• Pain management (also called pain medicine, or algiatry) is the medical discipline concerned with the relief of pain.
• <color=#3366CC>Pharmacogenomics</color> is a form of individualized medicine.
• <color=#3366CC>Podiatric medicine</color> is the study of, diagnosis, and medical treatment of disorders of the foot, ankle, lower limb, hip
and lower back.
• Sexual medicine is concerned with diagnosing, assessing and treating all disorders related to sexuality.
• <color=#3366CC>Sports medicine</color> deals with the treatment and prevention and rehabilitation of sports/exercise injuries such as
muscle spasms, <color=#3366CC>muscle tears</color>, injuries to ligaments (ligament tears or ruptures) and their repair in <color=#3366CC>athletes</color>, amateur
and professional.
• <color=#3366CC>Therapeutics</color> is the field, more commonly referenced in earlier periods of history, of the various remedies that can
be used to treat disease and promote health.
• Travel medicine or emporiatrics deals with health problems of international travelers or travelers across highly
different environments.
• Tropical medicine deals with the prevention and treatment of tropical diseases. It is studied separately in temperate
climates where those diseases are quite unfamiliar to medical practitioners and their local clinical needs.
• Urgent care focuses on delivery of unscheduled, walk-in care outside of the hospital emergency department for
injuries and illnesses that are not severe enough to require care in an emergency department. In some jurisdictions
this function is combined with the emergency department.
• <color=#3366CC>Veterinary medicine</color>; <color=#3366CC>veterinarians</color> apply similar techniques as physicians to the care of non-human animals.
• Wilderness medicine entails the practice of medicine in the wild, where conventional medical facilities may not be
available.
Education and legal controls
Medical education and training varies around the world. It typically involves entry level education at a university <color=#3366CC>medical</color>
<color=#3366CC>school</color>, followed by a period of supervised practice or internship, or residency. This can be followed by postgraduate
vocational training. A variety of teaching methods have been employed in medical education, still itself a focus of active
research. In Canada and the United States of America, a Doctor of Medicine degree, often abbreviated M.D., or a
Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine degree, often abbreviated as D.O. and unique to the United States, must be completed
in and delivered from a recognized university.
Since knowledge, techniques, and medical technology continue to evolve at a rapid rate, many regulatory authorities
require continuing medical education. Medical practitioners upgrade their knowledge in various ways, including medical
journals, seminars, conferences, and online programs. A database of objectives covering medical knowledge, as
suggested by national societies across the United States, can be searched at http://data.medobjectives.marian.edu/.
In most countries, it is a legal requirement for a medical doctor to be licensed or registered. In general, this entails a
medical degree from a university and accreditation by a medical board or an equivalent national organization, which
may ask the applicant to pass exams. This restricts the considerable legal authority of the medical profession to
physicians that are trained and qualified by national standards. It is also intended as an assurance to patients and as a
safeguard against charlatans that practice inadequate medicine for personal gain. While the laws generally require
medical doctors to be trained in "evidence based", Western, or <color=#3366CC>Hippocratic</color> Medicine, they are not intended to
discourage different paradigms of health.
In the European Union, the profession of doctor of medicine is regulated. A profession is said to be regulated when
access and exercise is subject to the possession of a specific professional qualification. The regulated professions
database contains a list of regulated professions for doctor of medicine in the EU member states, EEA countries and
Switzerland. This list is covered by the Directive 2005/36/EC.
Doctors who are negligent or intentionally harmful in their care of patients can face charges of medical malpractice and
be subject to civil, criminal, or professional sanctions.
Medical ethics
Medical ethics is a system of moral principles that apply values and judgments to the practice of medicine. As a
scholarly discipline, medical ethics encompasses its practical application in clinical settings as well as work on its
history, philosophy, theology, and sociology. Six of the values that commonly apply to medical ethics discussions are:
• <color=#3366CC>autonomy</color> – the patient has the right to refuse or choose their treatment. (Latin: Voluntas aegroti suprema lex.)
• beneficence – a practitioner should act in the best interest of the patient. (Latin: Salus aegroti suprema lex.)
• justice – concerns the distribution of scarce health resources, and the decision of who gets what treatment
(fairness and equality).
• non-maleficence – "first, do no harm" (Latin: primum non-nocere).
• respect for persons – the patient (and the person treating the patient) have the right to be treated with dignity.
• <color=#3366CC>truthfulness</color> and honesty – the concept of informed consent has increased in importance since the historical events
of the Doctors' Trial of the Nuremberg trials, <color=#3366CC>Tuskegee syphilis experiment</color>, and others.
Such values do not give answers as to how to handle a particular situation, but provide a useful framework for
understanding conflicts. When moral values are in conflict, the result may be an ethical dilemma or crisis. Sometimes,
no good solution to a dilemma in medical ethics exists, and occasionally, the values of the medical community (i.e., the
hospital and its staff) conflict with the values of the individual patient, family, or larger non-medical community. Conflicts
can also arise between health care providers or among family members. For example, some argue that the principles
of autonomy and beneficence clash when patients refuse <color=#3366CC>blood transfusions</color>, considering them life-saving; and
truth-telling was not emphasized to a large extent before the HIV era.
History
Ancient world
Prehistoric medicine incorporated plants (<color=#3366CC>herbalism</color>), animal parts, and minerals. In many cases these materials were
used ritually as magical substances by priests, <color=#3366CC>shamans</color>, or medicine men. Well-known spiritual systems include
<color=#3366CC>animism</color> (the notion of inanimate objects having spirits), spiritualism (an appeal to gods or communion with ancestor
spirits); <color=#3366CC>shamanism</color> (the vesting of an individual with mystic powers); and <color=#3366CC>divination</color> (magically obtaining the truth). The
field of medical anthropology examines the ways in which culture and society are organized around or impacted by
issues of health, health care and related issues.
The earliest known medical texts in the world were found in the ancient <color=#3366CC>Syrian</color> city of <color=#3366CC>Ebla</color> and date back to 2500 BCE.
Other early records on medicine have been discovered from <color=#3366CC>ancient Egyptian medicine</color>, <color=#3366CC>Babylonian Medicine</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Ayurvedic</color> medicine (in the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>), <color=#3366CC>classical Chinese medicine</color> (<color=#3366CC>Alternative medicine</color>) predecessor to the
modern <color=#3366CC>traditional Chinese medicine</color>), and <color=#3366CC>ancient Greek medicine</color> and Roman medicine.
In Egypt, <color=#3366CC>Imhotep</color> (3rd millennium BCE) is the first physician in history known by name. The oldest Egyptian medical
text is the Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus from around 2000 BCE, which describes gynaecological diseases. The
<color=#3366CC>Edwin Smith Papyrus</color> dating back to 1600 BCE is an early work on surgery, while the Ebers Papyrus dating back to
1500 BCE is akin to a textbook on medicine.
In China, archaeological evidence of medicine in Chinese dates back to the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color> <color=#3366CC>Shang dynasty</color>, based on
seeds for herbalism and tools presumed to have been used for surgery. The <color=#3366CC>Huangdi Neijing</color>, the progenitor of Chinese
medicine, is a medical text written beginning in the 2nd century BCE and compiled in the 3rd century.
In India, the oldest known surgical text, the Sushruta Samhita written by the surgeon <color=#3366CC>Sushruta</color>, described numerous
surgical operations, including the earliest forms of <color=#3366CC>plastic surgery</color> as well as methods of sterilization for surgical
instruments. The earliest records of dedicated hospitals come from Mihintale in <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color> where evidence of dedicated
medicinal treatment facilities for patients are found.
In Greece, the ancient Greek physician <color=#3366CC>Hippocrates</color>, the "father of modern medicine", laid the foundation for a rational
approach to medicine. Hippocrates introduced the Hippocratic Oath for physicians, which is still relevant and in use
today, and was the first to categorize illnesses as <color=#3366CC>acute</color>, <color=#3366CC>chronic</color>, endemic and epidemic, and use terms such as,
"exacerbation, relapse, resolution, crisis, paroxysm, peak, and convalescence". The Greek physician <color=#3366CC>Galen</color> was also
one of the greatest surgeons of the ancient world and performed many audacious operations, including brain and eye
surgeries. After the fall of the <color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color> and the onset of the <color=#3366CC>Early Middle Ages</color>, the Greek tradition of
medicine went into decline in Western Europe, although it continued uninterrupted in the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Roman (Byzantine)</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>.
Most of our knowledge of ancient Hebrew medicine during the 1st millennium BC comes from the <color=#3366CC>Torah</color>, i.e. the Five
Books of <color=#3366CC>Moses</color>, which contain various health related laws and rituals. The Hebrew contribution to the development of
modern medicine started in the Byzantine Era, with the physician Asaph the Jew.
Middle Ages
The concept of hospital as institution to offer medical care and possibility of a cure for the patients due to the ideals of
Christian charity, rather than just merely a place to die, appeared in the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>.
Although the concept of uroscopy was known to Galen, he did not see the importance of using it to localize the disease.
It was under the Byzantines with physicians such of Theophilus Protospatharius that they realized the potential in
uroscopy to determine disease in a time when no microscope or stethoscope existed. That practice eventually spread
to the rest of Europe.
After 750 CE, the Muslim world had the works of Hippocrates, Galen and Sushruta translated into <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Islamic</color>
<color=#3366CC>physicians</color> engaged in some significant medical research. Notable Islamic medical pioneers include the Persian
<color=#3366CC>polymath</color>, <color=#3366CC>Avicenna</color>, who, along with Imhotep and Hippocrates, has also been called the "father of medicine". He wrote
<color=#3366CC>The Canon of Medicine</color> which became a standard medical text at many medieval European <color=#3366CC>universities</color>, considered
one of the most famous books in the history of medicine. Others include <color=#3366CC>Abulcasis</color>, Avenzoar, <color=#3366CC>Ibn al-Nafis</color>, and

<color=#3366CC>Averroes</color>. <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> physician <color=#3366CC>Rhazes</color> was one of the first to question the Greek theory of <color=#3366CC>humorism</color>, which nevertheless
remained influential in both medieval Western and medieval Islamic medicine. Some volumes of Rhazes's work
Al-Mansuri, namely "On Surgery" and "A General Book on Therapy", became part of the medical curriculum in
European universities. Additionally, he has been described as a doctor's doctor, the father of pediatrics, and a pioneer
of ophthalmology. For example, he was the first to recognize the reaction of the eye's pupil to light. The Persian
Bimaristan hospitals were an early example of public hospitals.
In Europe, <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> decreed that a hospital should be attached to each cathedral and monastery and the historian
<color=#3366CC>Geoffrey Blainey</color> likened the activities of the Catholic Church in health care during the Middle Ages to an early version
of a welfare state: "It conducted hospitals for the old and orphanages for the young; hospices for the sick of all ages;
places for the lepers; and hostels or inns where pilgrims could buy a cheap bed and meal". It supplied food to the
population during famine and distributed food to the poor. This welfare system the church funded through collecting
taxes on a large scale and possessing large farmlands and estates. The <color=#3366CC>Benedictine</color> order was noted for setting up
hospitals and infirmaries in their monasteries, growing medical herbs and becoming the chief medical care givers of
their districts, as at the great <color=#3366CC>Abbey of Cluny</color>. The Church also established a network of cathedral schools and
universities where medicine was studied. The Schola Medica Salernitana in Salerno, looking to the learning of Greek
and <color=#3366CC>Arab</color> physicians, grew to be the finest medical school in medieval Europe.
However, the fourteenth and fifteenth century <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> devastated both the Middle East and Europe, and it has
even been argued that Western Europe was generally more effective in recovering from the pandemic than the Middle
East. In the early modern period, important early figures in medicine and anatomy emerged in Europe, including
<color=#3366CC>Gabriele Falloppio</color> and <color=#3366CC>William Harvey</color>.
The major shift in medical thinking was the gradual rejection, especially during the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> in the 14th and 15th
centuries, of what may be called the "traditional authority" approach to science and medicine. This was the notion that
because some prominent person in the past said something must be so, then that was the way it was, and anything
one observed to the contrary was an anomaly (which was paralleled by a similar shift in European society in general –
see <color=#3366CC>Copernicus</color>'s rejection of <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color>'s theories on astronomy). Physicians like <color=#3366CC>Vesalius</color> improved upon or disproved
some of the theories from the past. The main tomes used both by medicine students and expert physicians were De
materia medica and Pharmacopoeia.
<color=#3366CC>Andreas Vesalius</color> was the author of De humani corporis fabrica, an important book on <color=#3366CC>human anatomy</color>. Bacteria and
microorganisms were first observed with a microscope by <color=#3366CC>Antonie van Leeuwenhoek</color> in 1676, initiating the scientific
field <color=#3366CC>microbiology</color>. Independently from Ibn al-Nafis, <color=#3366CC>Michael Servetus</color> rediscovered the pulmonary circulation, but this
discovery did not reach the public because it was written down for the first time in the "Manuscript of Paris" in 1546, and
later published in the theological work for which he paid with his life in 1553. Later this was described by Renaldus
Columbus and Andrea Cesalpino. Herman Boerhaave is sometimes referred to as a "father of physiology" due to his
exemplary teaching in Leiden and textbook 'Institutiones medicae' (1708). <color=#3366CC>Pierre Fauchard</color> has been called "the father
of modern <color=#3366CC>dentistry</color>".
Modern
Veterinary medicine was, for the first time, truly separated from human medicine in 1761, when the French veterinarian
Claude Bourgelat founded the world's first veterinary school in Lyon, France. Before this, medical doctors treated both
humans and other animals.
Modern scientific biomedical research (where results are testable and <color=#3366CC>reproducible</color>) began to replace early Western
traditions based on herbalism, the Greek "four humours" and other such pre-modern notions. The modern era really
began with <color=#3366CC>Edward Jenner</color>'s discovery of the <color=#3366CC>smallpox vaccine</color> at the end of the 18th century (inspired by the method of
variolation originated in ancient China), <color=#3366CC>Robert Koch</color>'s discoveries around 1880 of the transmission of disease by
bacteria, and then the discovery of <color=#3366CC>antibiotics</color> around 1900.
The post-18th century <color=#3366CC>modernity</color> period brought more groundbreaking researchers from Europe. From <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> and
Austria, doctors <color=#3366CC>Rudolf Virchow</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen</color>, <color=#3366CC>Karl Landsteiner</color> and Otto Loewi made notable

contributions. In the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alexander Fleming</color>, <color=#3366CC>Joseph Lister</color>, <color=#3366CC>Francis Crick</color> and <color=#3366CC>Florence Nightingale</color> are
considered important. <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> doctor <color=#3366CC>Santiago Ramón y Cajal</color> is considered the father of modern <color=#3366CC>neuroscience</color>.
From New Zealand and Australia came <color=#3366CC>Maurice Wilkins</color>, <color=#3366CC>Howard Florey</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Frank Macfarlane Burnet</color>.
Others that did significant work include William Williams Keen, William Coley, <color=#3366CC>James D. Watson</color> (United States);

Salvador Luria (Italy); <color=#3366CC>Alexandre Yersin</color> (Switzerland); <color=#3366CC>Kitasato Shibasaburō</color> (Japan); <color=#3366CC>Jean-Martin Charcot</color>, <color=#3366CC>Claude</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bernard</color>, Paul Broca (France); Adolfo Lutz (Brazil); Nikolai Korotkov (Russia); <color=#3366CC>Sir William Osler</color> (Canada); and <color=#3366CC>Harvey</color>
<color=#3366CC>Cushing</color> (United States).
As science and technology developed, medicine became more reliant upon <color=#3366CC>medications</color>. Throughout history and in
Europe right until the late 18th century, not only plant products were used as medicine, but also animal (including
human) body parts and fluids. <color=#3366CC>Pharmacology</color> developed in part from herbalism and some drugs are still derived from

plants (<color=#3366CC>atropine</color>, <color=#3366CC>ephedrine</color>, <color=#3366CC>warfarin</color>, <color=#3366CC>aspirin</color>, digoxin, vinca alkaloids, taxol, <color=#3366CC>hyoscine</color>, etc.). <color=#3366CC>Vaccines</color> were discovered
by Edward Jenner and <color=#3366CC>Louis Pasteur</color>.
The first antibiotic was arsphenamine (Salvarsan) discovered by <color=#3366CC>Paul Ehrlich</color> in 1908 after he observed that bacteria
took up toxic dyes that human cells did not. The first major class of antibiotics was the sulfa drugs, derived by German
chemists originally from azo dyes.
Pharmacology has become increasingly sophisticated; modern <color=#3366CC>biotechnology</color> allows drugs targeted towards specific
physiological processes to be developed, sometimes designed for compatibility with the body to reduce <color=#3366CC>side-effects</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Genomics</color> and knowledge of human genetics and <color=#3366CC>human evolution</color> is having increasingly significant influence on
medicine, as the causative <color=#3366CC>genes</color> of most monogenic <color=#3366CC>genetic disorders</color> have now been identified, and the development
of techniques in <color=#3366CC>molecular biology</color>, <color=#3366CC>evolution</color>, and <color=#3366CC>genetics</color> are influencing medical technology, practice and
decision-making.
Evidence-based medicine is a contemporary movement to establish the most effective <color=#3366CC>algorithms</color> of practice (ways of
doing things) through the use of systematic reviews and meta-analysis. The movement is facilitated by modern global
<color=#3366CC>information science</color>, which allows as much of the available evidence as possible to be collected and analyzed
according to standard protocols that are then disseminated to healthcare providers. The Cochrane Collaboration leads
this movement. A 2001 review of 160 Cochrane systematic reviews revealed that, according to two readers, 21.3% of
the reviews concluded insufficient evidence, 20% concluded evidence of no effect, and 22.5% concluded positive
effect.
Quality, efficiency, and access
Evidence-based medicine, prevention of medical error (and other "iatrogenesis"), and avoidance of unnecessary health
care are a priority in modern medical systems. These topics generate significant political and public policy attention,
particularly in the United States where healthcare is regarded as excessively costly but population health metrics lag
similar nations.
Health spending varies by country, which results in differences in access to care and access to medicines. Health care
rationing varies by country. Most developed countries provide health care to all citizens, with a few exceptions such as
the United States where restrictions on <color=#3366CC>health insurance</color> coverage may limit affordability.
Telemedicine
Telemedicine (also Telehealth) refers to preventive, promotive, and curative care delivery, including remote clinical
services, such as diagnosis, monitoring, administration and provider education. The main categories of telehealth:
• Telenursing is experiencing significant growth globally due to factors such as the need to reduce healthcare costs,
an increasing aging and chronically ill population, and expanded healthcare coverage to distant, rural, small, or
sparsely populated regions. Telenursing can help address nurse shortages, reduce travel time and distances, and
minimize hospital admissions.
• <color=#3366CC>Telepalliative care</color> is a remote approach to optimising quality of life and relieving suffering for people with serious,
complex and often fatal illnesses. The <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization</color> (WHO) recommends integrating palliative care as
early as possible for any chronic and fatal illness. Telepalliative care typically utilizes telecommunication
technologies like video conferencing, messaging for follow-ups, and digital symptom assessments through
questionnaires that generate alerts for healthcare professionals.
• Telepharmacy involves delivering pharmaceutical care via telecommunications to patients in locations where direct
contact with a pharmacist may not be possible or difficult.
• Telepsychiatry (telemental health) uses telecommunications technology to provide remote psychiatric care for
individuals with mental health conditions.
• Telepsychology is the use of communication technology for the remote administration of psychological tests and
psychotherapy.
• Teleneurotherapy utilizes computers and communications technology to deliver neurotherapy remotely. Research
indicates that systematic physical stimuli from standard electronic devices, such as tablets with headphones, may
treat injured nervous systems online by modulating neuronal plasticity. Evidence suggests that teleneurotherapy
could enhance neurological treatment if it incorporates the therapeutic effect of a systematic abiotic impact of
physical forces with key parameters of mother-fetus interaction. Recent research has shown therapeutic effects
when implementing the APIN method in the online treatment of patients with various neurological conditions.
• Telenutrition refers to the use of video conferencing or telephony to provide online consultations by nutritionists or
dieticians.
• Telerehabilitation (or e-rehabilitation) is the delivery of rehabilitation services over telecommunication networks and
the Internet. Most services fall into two categories: clinical assessment (evaluating the patient's functional abilities
in their environment) and clinical therapy.
Nuclear fusion
Nuclear fusion is a <color=#3366CC>reaction</color> in which two or more <color=#3366CC>atomic nuclei</color> combine to form a larger nucleus. The difference in
mass between the reactants and products is manifested as either the release or the <color=#3366CC>absorption</color> of <color=#3366CC>energy</color>. This
difference in mass arises as a result of the difference in <color=#3366CC>nuclear binding energy</color> between the atomic nuclei before and

after the fusion reaction. Active <color=#3366CC>stellar cores</color> are powered by fusion. <color=#3366CC>Nucleosynthesis</color> via fusion, <color=#3366CC>in the Big Bang</color> and <color=#3366CC>in</color>
<color=#3366CC>stars</color>, creates all elements lighter than <color=#3366CC>nickel</color> (<color=#3366CC>atomic number</color> 28).
Fusion typically occurs via thermonuclear fusion, an isotropic process requiring a triple product of very high
temperature (in the <color=#3366CC>kiloelectronvolt</color> or hundred million <color=#3366CC>Kelvin</color> range), density, and confinement time. These conditions
occur only in, <color=#3366CC>thermonuclear weapons</color> and boosted fission weapons, and <color=#3366CC>fusion power</color> experiments.
A nuclear fusion process that produces atomic nuclei lighter than nickel-62 is generally <color=#3366CC>exothermic</color>, due to the positive
gradient of the <color=#3366CC>nuclear binding energy curve</color>. The most fusible nuclei are among the lightest, especially <color=#3366CC>deuterium</color>,
<color=#3366CC>tritium</color>, and <color=#3366CC>helium-3</color>. The opposite process, <color=#3366CC>nuclear fission</color>, is most energetic for very heavy nuclei, especially the
<color=#3366CC>actinides</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Fusion power</color> seeks to use fusion for <color=#3366CC>energy development</color>; <color=#3366CC>tokamaks</color> and stellarators are the dominant designs in
magnetic confinement fusion research. Fusion devices can also be used as neutron sources and in <color=#3366CC>superheavy</color>
<color=#3366CC>element</color> production.
History
Theory
American chemist William Draper Harkins was the first to propose the concept of nuclear fusion in 1915. <color=#3366CC>Francis</color>
<color=#3366CC>William Aston</color>'s 1919 invention of the <color=#3366CC>mass spectrometer</color> allowed the discovery that four hydrogen atoms are heavier
than one helium atom. Thus in 1920, <color=#3366CC>Arthur Eddington</color> correctly predicted fusion of hydrogen into helium could be the
primary source of stellar energy.
<color=#3366CC>Quantum tunneling</color> was discovered by Friedrich Hund in 1927, with relation to electron levels. In 1928, George Gamow
was the first to apply tunneling to the nucleus, first to <color=#3366CC>alpha decay</color>, then to fusion as an inverse process. From this, in
1929, Robert Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans made the first estimates for stellar fusion rates.
In 1938, <color=#3366CC>Hans Bethe</color> worked with Charles Critchfield to enumerate the <color=#3366CC>proton–proton chain</color> that dominates Sun-type
stars. In 1939, Bethe published the discovery of the <color=#3366CC>CNO cycle</color> common to higher-mass stars.
Early experiments
During the 1920s, <color=#3366CC>Patrick Blackett</color> made the first conclusive experiments in artificial nuclear transmutation at the
Cavendish Laboratory. There, <color=#3366CC>John Cockcroft</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ernest Walton</color> built their generator on the inspiration of Gamow's
paper. In April 1932, they published experiments on the reaction:
+ <color=#3366CC>p</color> 2 where the intermediary nuclide was later confirmed to be the extremely short-lived beryllium-8. This has a claim to
the first artificial fusion reaction.
In papers from July and November 1933, <color=#3366CC>Ernest Lawrence</color> et al. at the University of California Radiation Laboratory, in
some of the earliest cyclotron experiments, accidentally produced the first <color=#3366CC>deuterium–deuterium fusion</color> reactions: + + p
The Radiation Lab, only detecting the resulting energized protons and neutrons, misinterpreted the source as an
exothermic disintegration of the deuterons, now known to be impossible. In May 1934, <color=#3366CC>Mark Oliphant</color>, Paul Harteck,
and <color=#3366CC>Ernest Rutherford</color> at the Cavendish Laboratory, published an intentional deuterium fusion experiment, and made
the discovery of both <color=#3366CC>tritium</color> and <color=#3366CC>helium-3</color>. This is widely considered the first experimental demonstration of fusion.
In 1938, Arthur Ruhlig at the University of Michigan made the first observation of deuterium–tritium (DT) fusion and its
characteristic 14 MeV neutrons, now known as the most favourable reaction: + +
Weaponization
Research into <color=#3366CC>fusion for military purposes</color> began in the early 1940s as part of the <color=#3366CC>Manhattan Project</color>. In 1941, Enrico
Fermi and Edward Teller had a conversation about the possibility of a fission bomb creating conditions for
thermonuclear fusion. In 1942, Emil Konopinski brought Ruhlig's work on the deuterium–tritium reaction to the project's
attention. <color=#3366CC>J. Robert Oppenheimer</color> initially commissioned physicists at Chicago and Cornell to use the Harvard
University cyclotron to secretly investigate its cross-section, and that of the lithium reaction (see below). Measurements
were obtained at Purdue, Chicago, and Los Alamos from 1942 to 1946. Theoretical assumptions about DT fusion gave
it a similar cross-section to DD. However, in 1946 Egon Bretscher discovered a resonance enhancement giving the DT
reaction a cross-section ~100 times larger.
From 1945, John von Neumann, Teller, and other Los Alamos scientists used <color=#3366CC>ENIAC</color>, one of the first electronic
computers, to simulate thermonuclear weapon detonations. In January 1950, several months after the first Soviet
fission test was detected, the US announced a crash program to develop the hydrogen bomb. Initial theoretical efforts
were focused on the idea of a self-sustaining fusion reaction in a "pipe" of (uncompressed) liquid deuterium, initiated by
a fission bomb and a small amount of deuterium-tritium fusion at one end of the bomb. But calculations and
computations made shortly after the announcement showed that this approach was unlikely to work: even if deuterium
fusion was achieved in such a scheme, energy losses would immediately halt the progress of the reaction. A search for
new ideas led to the Teller-Ulam design, named after Teller and <color=#3366CC>Stanislaw Ulam</color>, which used the radiation energy of a
fission bomb to highly compress (radiation implosion) the fusion fuel prior to its ignition. This was accomplished by
physically separating the fission ("primary") and thermonuclear ("secondary") components and placing them within a
casing that would contain and re-direct the radiation energy appropriately.
The concept was first tested during the May 1951 US Greenhouse George nuclear test, using a small amount of
deuterium–tritium gas. The device produced the largest explosive yield to date, at 225 <color=#3366CC>kilotons</color>, essentially all from
fission, but the experimental results validated the fundamental concept. Another test during the Greenhouse series,
Greenhouse Item, also demonstrated a concept known as "boosting", in which a small amount of a deuterium-tritium
mixture was inserted into the center of an <color=#3366CC>implosion-type</color> fission weapon. The detonation of the weapon induced a
small amount of nuclear fusion, but the neutrons from the fusion reaction greatly increased the efficiency of the fission
reaction, doubling its explosive output.
A full proof-of-concept of the Teller-Ulam design was demonstrated in the November 1952 Ivy Mike test. This was a
full-sized <color=#3366CC>liquid</color> deuterium-fusing two-stage test, designed by Richard Garwin, and yielded over 10 <color=#3366CC>megatons</color> of TNT
equivalent. Over 70% of the explosion yield was from fission, mostly from the fast-fissioning of a uranium tamper by the
neutrons produced from the deuterium fusion. It was not a deliverable weapon, as the cryogenic equipment necessary
for keeping the deuterium in a liquid phase weighed 80 tons.
The Soviet Union had their own hydrogen bomb program. In August 1953, they carried out a test of a bomb known as
RDS-6s. This was a type of "boosted" weapon, albeit one which used much more fusion than the American approach. It
used a solid fuel, <color=#3366CC>lithium deuteride</color>, as its fusion fuel. It yielded 400 kt, of which 20% was from fusion. As a single-stage
weapon, it lacked the efficiency and flexibility that two-stage weapons promised, but could be deployed immediately.
Lithium deuteride had been identified by both the US and Soviet Union as a potential fusion fuel for weapons. Because
it was solid, it would not require cryogenics to use effectively in large weapons. The lithium-6 isotope was particularly
reactive, and could be used to generate tritium exothermically via the Jetter cycle:
+ + During thermonuclear detonations, this provides tritium for the highly energetic DT reaction, and benefits from its
neutron production, creating a closed neutron cycle.
The United States tested a deliverable, lithium-deuteride device in 1954. Castle Bravo had an unexpectedly high yield
of 15 Mt, and generated significant amounts of <color=#3366CC>nuclear fallout</color> contamination. The Soviets tested their first two-stage
device, RDS-37, in 1955, with a yield of 1.5 Mt, having apparently independently discovered the principle. Later
innovation in nuclear weapons would allow two-stage weapons to be significantly miniaturized.
Fusion energy
While fusion bomb detonations were loosely considered for energy production, the possibility of controlled and
sustained reactions remained the scientific focus for peaceful fusion power. Research into developing controlled fusion
inside <color=#3366CC>fusion reactors</color> has been ongoing since the 1930s, with <color=#3366CC>Los Alamos National Laboratory</color>'s Scylla I device
producing the first laboratory thermonuclear fusion in 1958, but the technology is still in its developmental phase.
The first experiments producing large amounts of controlled fusion power were the experiments with mixes of
deuterium and tritium in <color=#3366CC>Tokamaks</color>. Experiments in the TFTR at the PPPL in <color=#3366CC>Princeton University</color> Princeton NJ, USA
during 1993–1996 produced 1.6 GJ of fusion energy. The peak fusion power was 10.3 MW from 3.7×10^18 reactions
per second, and peak fusion energy created in one discharge was 7.6 MJ. Subsequent experiments in the JET in 1997
achieved a peak fusion power of 16 MW (5.8×10^18 s). The central Q, defined as the local fusion power produced to
the local applied heating power, is computed to be 1.3. A JET experiment in 2024 produced 69 MJ of fusion power,
consuming 0.2 mgm of D and T.
The US National Ignition Facility, which uses laser-driven <color=#3366CC>inertial confinement fusion</color>, was designed with a goal of
achieving a fusion energy gain factor (Q) of larger than one; the first large-scale laser target experiments were
performed in June 2009 and ignition experiments began in early 2011. On 13 December 2022, the United States
Department of Energy announced that on 5 December 2022, they had successfully accomplished break-even fusion,
"delivering 2.05 megajoules (MJ) of energy to the target, resulting in 3.15 MJ of fusion energy output". The rate of
supplying power to the experimental test cell is hundreds of times larger than the power delivered to the target.
Prior to this breakthrough, controlled fusion reactions had been unable to produce break-even (self-sustaining)
controlled fusion. The two most advanced approaches for it are magnetic confinement (toroid designs) and inertial
confinement (laser designs). Workable designs for a toroidal reactor that theoretically will deliver ten times more fusion
energy than the amount needed to heat plasma to the required temperatures are in development (see ITER). The ITER
facility is currently expected to initiate plasma experiments in 2034, but is not expected to begin full deuterium–tritium
fusion until 2039.
Private companies pursuing the commercialization of nuclear fusion received $2.6 billion in private funding in 2021
alone, going to many notable startups including but not limited to Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Helion Energy Inc.,
General Fusion, TAE Technologies Inc. and Zap Energy Inc.
One of the most recent breakthroughs to date in maintaining a sustained fusion reaction occurred in France's WEST
fusion reactor. It maintained a 90 million degree plasma for a record time of six minutes. This is a tokamak-style reactor
which is the same style as the upcoming ITER reactor.
Process
The release of energy with the fusion of light elements is due to the interplay of two opposing forces: the <color=#3366CC>nuclear force</color>,
a manifestation of the <color=#3366CC>strong interaction</color>, which holds protons and neutrons tightly together in the <color=#3366CC>atomic nucleus</color>; and
the <color=#3366CC>Coulomb force</color>, which causes positively <color=#3366CC>charged</color> <color=#3366CC>protons</color> in the nucleus to repel each other. Lighter nuclei (nuclei
smaller than iron and nickel) are sufficiently small and proton-poor to allow the nuclear force to overcome the Coulomb
force. This is because the nucleus is sufficiently small that all nucleons feel the short-range attractive force at least as
strongly as they feel the infinite-range Coulomb repulsion. Building up nuclei from lighter nuclei by fusion releases the
extra energy from the net attraction of particles. For larger nuclei, however, no energy is released, because the nuclear
force is short-range and cannot act across larger nuclei.
Fusion powers <color=#3366CC>stars</color> and produces most elements lighter than cobalt in a process called <color=#3366CC>nucleosynthesis</color>. The Sun is a
main-sequence star, and, as such, generates its energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium. In its core,
the Sun fuses 620 million metric tons of hydrogen and makes 616 million metric tons of helium each second. The fusion
of lighter elements in stars releases energy and the mass that always accompanies it. For example, in the fusion of two
hydrogen nuclei to form helium, 0.645% of the mass is carried away in the form of kinetic energy of an <color=#3366CC>alpha particle</color> or
other forms of energy, such as electromagnetic radiation.
It takes considerable energy to force nuclei to fuse, even those of the lightest element, <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color>. When accelerated to
high enough speeds, nuclei can overcome this electrostatic repulsion and be brought close enough such that the
attractive <color=#3366CC>nuclear force</color> is greater than the repulsive Coulomb force. The <color=#3366CC>strong force</color> grows rapidly once the nuclei are
close enough, and the fusing nucleons can essentially "fall" into each other and the result is fusion; this is an
<color=#3366CC>exothermic process</color>.
Energy released in most <color=#3366CC>nuclear reactions</color> is much larger than in <color=#3366CC>chemical reactions</color>, because the <color=#3366CC>binding energy</color> that
holds a nucleus together is greater than the energy that holds <color=#3366CC>electrons</color> to a nucleus. For example, the <color=#3366CC>ionization</color>
<color=#3366CC>energy</color> gained by adding an electron to a hydrogen nucleus is 13.6 eV—less than one-millionth of the 17.6 MeV
released in the <color=#3366CC>deuterium</color>–<color=#3366CC>tritium</color> (D–T) reaction shown in the adjacent diagram. Fusion reactions have an <color=#3366CC>energy</color>
<color=#3366CC>density</color> many times greater than <color=#3366CC>nuclear fission</color>; the reactions produce far greater energy per unit of mass even though
individual fission reactions are generally much more energetic than individual fusion ones, which are themselves
millions of times more energetic than chemical reactions. Via the <color=#3366CC>mass–energy equivalence</color>, fusion yields a 0.7%
efficiency of reactant mass into energy. This can only be exceeded by the extreme cases of the <color=#3366CC>accretion</color> process
involving <color=#3366CC>neutron stars</color> or black holes, approaching 40% efficiency, and <color=#3366CC>antimatter</color> <color=#3366CC>annihilation</color> at 100% efficiency. (The
complete conversion of one gram of matter would expel 9×10^13 joules of energy.)
In astrophysics
Fusion is responsible for the astrophysical production of the majority of elements lighter than iron. This includes most
types of <color=#3366CC>Big Bang nucleosynthesis</color> and <color=#3366CC>stellar nucleosynthesis</color>. Non-fusion processes that contribute include the
<color=#3366CC>s-process</color> and <color=#3366CC>r-process</color> in neutron merger and <color=#3366CC>supernova nucleosynthesis</color>, responsible for elements heavier than iron.
Stars
An important fusion process is the <color=#3366CC>stellar nucleosynthesis</color> that powers <color=#3366CC>stars</color>, including the Sun. In the 20th century, it
was recognized that the energy released from nuclear fusion reactions accounts for the longevity of stellar heat and
light. The fusion of nuclei in a star, starting from its initial hydrogen and helium abundance, provides that energy and
synthesizes new nuclei. Different reaction chains are involved, depending on the mass of the star (and therefore the
pressure and temperature in its core).
Around 1920, <color=#3366CC>Arthur Eddington</color> anticipated the discovery and mechanism of nuclear fusion processes in stars, in his
paper The Internal Constitution of the Stars. At that time, the source of stellar energy was unknown; Eddington correctly
speculated that the source was fusion of hydrogen into helium, liberating enormous energy according to <color=#3366CC>Einstein's</color>
<color=#3366CC>equation</color>. This was a particularly remarkable development since at that time fusion and thermonuclear energy had not
yet been discovered, nor even that stars are largely composed of <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color>. Eddington's paper reasoned that:
• The leading theory of stellar energy, the contraction hypothesis, should cause the rotation of a star to visibly speed
up due to <color=#3366CC>conservation of angular momentum</color>. But observations of <color=#3366CC>Cepheid</color> variable stars showed this was not
happening.
• The only other known plausible source of energy was conversion of matter to energy; Einstein had shown some
years earlier that a small amount of matter was equivalent to a large amount of energy.
• <color=#3366CC>Francis Aston</color> had also shown that the mass of a helium atom was about 0.8% less than the mass of the four
hydrogen atoms which would, combined, form a helium atom (according to the then-prevailing theory of atomic
structure which held atomic weight to be the distinguishing property between elements; work by Henry Moseley
and Antonius van den Broek would later show that nucleic charge was the distinguishing property and that a helium
nucleus, therefore, consisted of two hydrogen nuclei plus additional mass). This suggested that if such a
combination could happen, it would release considerable energy as a byproduct.
• If a star contained just 5% of fusible hydrogen, it would suffice to explain how stars got their energy. (It is now
known that most 'ordinary' stars are usually made of around 70% to 75% hydrogen)
• Further elements might also be fused, and other scientists had speculated that stars were the "crucible" in which
light elements combined to create heavy elements, but without more accurate measurements of their <color=#3366CC>atomic</color>
<color=#3366CC>masses</color> nothing more could be said at the time.
All of these speculations were proven correct in the following decades.
The primary source of solar energy, and that of similar size stars, is the fusion of hydrogen to form helium (the
<color=#3366CC>proton–proton chain</color> reaction), which occurs at a solar-core temperature of 14 million kelvin. The net result is the fusion

of four <color=#3366CC>protons</color> into one <color=#3366CC>alpha particle</color>, with the release of two <color=#3366CC>positrons</color> and two <color=#3366CC>neutrinos</color> (which changes two of the
protons into neutrons), and energy. In heavier stars, the <color=#3366CC>CNO cycle</color> and other processes are more important. As a star
uses up a substantial fraction of its hydrogen, it begins to fuse heavier elements. In massive cores, silicon-burning is
the final fusion cycle, leading to a build-up of iron and nickel nuclei.
<color=#3366CC>Nuclear binding energy</color> makes the production of elements heavier than nickel via fusion energetically unfavorable.
These elements are produced in non-fusion processes: the <color=#3366CC>s-process</color>, <color=#3366CC>r-process</color>, and the variety of processes that can
produce p-nuclei. Such processes occur in giant star shells, or <color=#3366CC>supernovae</color>, or neutron star mergers.
Brown dwarfs
<color=#3366CC>Brown dwarfs</color> fuse deuterium and in very high mass cases also fuse lithium.
White dwarfs
Carbon–oxygen <color=#3366CC>white dwarfs</color>, which accrete matter either from an active stellar companion or white dwarf merger,
approach the <color=#3366CC>Chandrasekhar limit</color> of 1.44 solar masses. Immediately prior, <color=#3366CC>carbon burning</color> fusion begins, destroying
the Earth-sized dwarf within one second, in a <color=#3366CC>Type Ia supernova</color>.
Much more rarely, helium white dwarfs may merge, which does not cause an explosion but begins <color=#3366CC>helium burning</color> in an
extreme type of helium star.
Neutron stars
Some neutron stars accrete hydrogen and helium from an active stellar companion. Periodically, the helium accretion
reaches a critical level, and a thermonuclear burn wave propagates across the surface, on the timescale of one
second.
Black hole accretion disks
Similar to stellar fusion, extreme conditions within <color=#3366CC>black hole</color> <color=#3366CC>accretion disks</color> can allow fusion reactions. Calculations
show the most energetic reactions occur around lower <color=#3366CC>stellar mass black holes</color>, below 10 solar masses, compared to
those above 100. Beyond five <color=#3366CC>Schwarzschild radii</color>, <color=#3366CC>carbon-burning</color> and fusion of helium-3 dominates the reactions.
Within this distance, around lower mass black holes, fusion of nitrogen, oxygen, neon, and magnesium can occur. In
the extreme limit, the silicon-burning process can begin with the fusion of silicon and selenium nuclei.
Big Bang
From the period approximately 10 seconds to 20 minutes after the <color=#3366CC>Big Bang</color>, the universe cooled from over 100 keV to
1 keV. This allowed the combining of protons and neutrons into deuterium nuclei, and beginning a rapid fusion chain
into tritium and helium-3 and ending in predominantly helium-4, with a minimal fraction of lithium, beryllium, and boron
nuclei.
Observational evidence shows that pockets of gas in the <color=#3366CC>early universe</color> became thick enough to collapse under their
own <color=#3366CC>gravity</color>. This activated nuclear fusion with the formation of the first stars around 13.6 billion years ago.
Requirements
A substantial energy barrier of electrostatic forces must be overcome before fusion can occur. At large distances, two
naked nuclei repel one another because of the repulsive <color=#3366CC>electrostatic force</color> between their <color=#3366CC>positively charged</color> protons. If
two nuclei can be brought close enough together, however, the electrostatic repulsion can be overcome by the
quantum effect in which nuclei can <color=#3366CC>tunnel</color> through coulomb forces.
When a <color=#3366CC>nucleon</color> such as a <color=#3366CC>proton</color> or <color=#3366CC>neutron</color> is added to a nucleus, the nuclear force attracts it to all the other nucleons
of the nucleus (if the atom is small enough), but primarily to its immediate neighbors due to the short range of the force.
The nucleons in the interior of a nucleus have more neighboring nucleons than those on the surface. Since smaller
nuclei have a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio, the binding energy per nucleon due to the <color=#3366CC>nuclear force</color> generally
increases with the size of the nucleus but approaches a limiting value corresponding to that of a nucleus with a
diameter of about four nucleons. It is important to keep in mind that nucleons are <color=#3366CC>quantum objects</color>. So, for example,
since two neutrons in a nucleus are identical to each other, the goal of distinguishing one from the other, such as which
one is in the interior and which is on the surface, is in fact meaningless, and the inclusion of quantum mechanics is
therefore necessary for proper calculations.
The electrostatic force, on the other hand, is an <color=#3366CC>inverse-square force</color>, so a proton added to a nucleus will feel an
electrostatic repulsion from all the other protons in the nucleus. The electrostatic energy per nucleon due to the
electrostatic force thus increases without limit as nuclei atomic number grows.
The net result of the opposing electrostatic and strong nuclear forces is that the binding energy per nucleon generally
increases with increasing size, up to the elements <color=#3366CC>iron</color> and <color=#3366CC>nickel</color>, and then decreases for heavier nuclei. Eventually,
the <color=#3366CC>binding energy</color> becomes negative and very heavy nuclei (all with more than 208 nucleons, corresponding to a
diameter of about 6 nucleons) are not stable. The four most tightly bound nuclei, in decreasing order of <color=#3366CC>binding energy</color>
per nucleon, are, and. Even though the nickel isotope, is more stable, the iron isotope is an order of magnitude more
common. This is due to the fact that there is no easy way for stars to create through the alpha process.
An exception to this general trend is the <color=#3366CC>helium-4</color> nucleus, whose binding energy is higher than that of <color=#3366CC>lithium</color>, the next
heavier element. This is because protons and neutrons are <color=#3366CC>fermions</color>, which according to the <color=#3366CC>Pauli exclusion principle</color>
cannot exist in the same nucleus in exactly the same state. Each proton or neutron's energy state in a nucleus can
accommodate both a spin up particle and a spin down particle. Helium-4 has an anomalously large binding energy
because its nucleus consists of two protons and two neutrons (it is a doubly magic nucleus), so all four of its nucleons
can be in the ground state. Any additional nucleons would have to go into higher energy states. Indeed, the helium-4
nucleus is so tightly bound that it is commonly treated as a single quantum mechanical particle in nuclear physics,
namely, the <color=#3366CC>alpha particle</color>.
The situation is similar if two nuclei are brought together. As they approach each other, all the protons in one nucleus
repel all the protons in the other. Not until the two nuclei actually come close enough for long enough so the strong
attractive <color=#3366CC>nuclear force</color> can take over and overcome the repulsive electrostatic force. This can also be described as the
nuclei overcoming the so-called Coulomb barrier. The kinetic energy to achieve this can be lower than the barrier itself
because of quantum tunneling.
The Coulomb barrier is smallest for isotopes of hydrogen, as their nuclei contain only a single positive charge. A
diproton is not stable, so neutrons must also be involved, ideally in such a way that a helium nucleus, with its extremely
tight binding, is one of the products.
Using <color=#3366CC>deuterium–tritium</color> fuel, the resulting energy barrier is about 0.1 MeV. In comparison, the energy needed to
remove an <color=#3366CC>electron</color> from <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> is 13.6 eV. The (intermediate) result of the fusion is an unstable 5He nucleus, which
immediately ejects a neutron with 14.1 MeV. The recoil energy of the remaining 4He nucleus is 3.5 MeV, so the total
energy liberated is 17.6 MeV. This is many times more than what was needed to overcome the energy barrier.

two reactant nuclei. If the reactants have a distribution of velocities, e.g. a thermal distribution, then it is useful to
perform an average over the distributions of the product of cross-section and velocity. This average is called the
'reactivity', denoted ‹v›. The reaction rate (fusions per volume per time) is ‹v› times the product of the reactant number
densities:

these temperatures, well above typical <color=#3366CC>ionization</color> energies (13.6 eV in the hydrogen case), the fusion reactants exist in
